steps.title: Import TypeScript types and interfaces needed for mock data
steps.instruction: Create two TypeScript interfaces named 'User' and 'Product' that define the shape of our mock data. Place them at the top of your file.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and define properties inside curly braces.
steps.seedCode: // Create your User and Product interfaces here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have two TypeScript interfaces ready to use for building typed mock data.
successCriteria: The file contains a 'User' interface and a 'Product' interface with appropriate property definitions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the TypeScript interfaces that will serve as the foundation for our typed mock data builders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created both interfaces with proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword and define properties for both User and Product.

steps.title: Create the User interface type definition
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'User' with the following properties: 'id' (number), 'name' (string), 'email' (string), and 'isActive' (boolean).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with their types.
steps.expectedOutcome: The User interface is defined with correct property types.
successCriteria: The User interface exists with id (number), name (string), email (string), and isActive (boolean) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the User interface with proper TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure all four properties (id, name, email, isActive) are defined with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface definition is incomplete or has incorrect types. Check the property names and their TypeScript types.

steps.title: Create the Product interface type definition
steps.instruction: Define a Product interface with id (number), title (string), price (number), and inStock (boolean) properties using TypeScript types.
steps.hint: Start with 'interface Product {' then add each property with its type annotation, like 'id: number;'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Product interface with four typed properties is added to the code.
successCriteria: Product interface is defined with id: number, title: string, price: number, and inStock: boolean.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the Product interface with all required properties and correct TypeScript types.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the Product interface, but some properties are missing or have incorrect types. Check that you have id (number), title (string), price (number), and inStock (boolean).
steps.feedbackWrong: The Product interface is not properly defined. Make sure you create an interface named Product with the four specified properties and their TypeScript types.

steps.title: Create the base mockUserBuilder function
steps.instruction: Create a function named mockUserBuilder that returns a User object with default values. The function should have no parameters and return a User object with placeholder values for all required properties.
steps.hint: Define a function that returns an object matching the User interface. Use placeholder values like empty strings, 0, or false for the properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A mockUserBuilder function is created that returns a User object with default values for all properties.
successCriteria: The mockUserBuilder function exists, has no parameters, and returns an object with all User interface properties populated with placeholder values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the base mockUserBuilder function that returns a properly typed User object with default values.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but it might be missing some required User properties or the return type doesn't match the User interface. Make sure all User properties are included with placeholder values.
steps.feedbackWrong: The mockUserBuilder function is not properly defined. Create a function named mockUserBuilder that returns a User object with all required properties filled with default values.

steps.title: Add optional overrides parameter to mockUserBuilder
steps.instruction: Add a parameter named 'overrides' to the mockUserBuilder function signature. The parameter should be typed as Partial<User> and be optional (use a default value of an empty object {}).
steps.hint: Add the parameter inside the parentheses after the function name. Use TypeScript's Partial utility type to make all properties optional.
steps.expectedOutcome: The mockUserBuilder function should accept an optional overrides parameter that allows partial User objects to be passed in.
successCriteria: mockUserBuilder function has an optional 'overrides' parameter typed as Partial<User> with a default value of {}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the optional overrides parameter with the correct TypeScript type. This will allow users to override specific properties when creating mock users.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your parameter is typed as Partial<User> and has a default value of an empty object {}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature doesn't match what's needed. Remember to add an optional 'overrides' parameter with type Partial<User> and a default value of {}.

steps.title: Implement the override logic in mockUserBuilder
steps.instruction: Update the mockUserBuilder function to accept an optional overrides parameter and merge it with the default user object using object spread syntax.
steps.hint: Add a parameter to the function signature and use the spread operator to combine defaultUser with overrides in the return statement.
steps.expectedOutcome: The mockUserBuilder function now accepts optional overrides and merges them with the default user object.
successCriteria: mockUserBuilder has an optional overrides parameter of type Partial<User> and returns the merged object using spread syntax.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the override logic using object spread.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the overrides parameter is optional and uses Partial<User>, and that you're merging with spread syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The override logic isn't implemented correctly. Check the function signature and the merging syntax.

steps.title: Create the base mockProductBuilder function
steps.instruction: Create a function named mockProductBuilder that returns a Product object with default values.
steps.hint: Define the function with default values for id, name, and price. Use the Product interface you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: A mockProductBuilder function is created that returns a Product object with default values.
successCriteria: The mockProductBuilder function exists and returns a Product object with default values for id, name, and price.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the mockProductBuilder function. This follows the same pattern as mockUserBuilder but for a different data type.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function returns a Product object with default values for id, name, and price.
steps.feedbackWrong: The mockProductBuilder function should return a Product object with default values. Check that you've defined the function correctly.

steps.title: Add optional overrides parameter to mockProductBuilder
steps.instruction: Add an optional overrides parameter to the mockProductBuilder function signature. The parameter should be typed as Partial<Product> and have a default value of an empty object {}.
steps.hint: Modify the function signature to accept a parameter with type Partial<Product> and default it to {}.
steps.expectedOutcome: The mockProductBuilder function signature now accepts an optional overrides parameter typed as Partial<Product> with a default empty object.
successCriteria: mockProductBuilder function has an optional overrides parameter with type Partial<Product> and default value {}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the optional overrides parameter to mockProductBuilder, allowing future customization of product data.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a parameter, but check: is it typed as Partial<Product> and does it have a default value of {}?
steps.feedbackWrong: The mockProductBuilder function signature doesn't yet have the optional overrides parameter with type Partial<Product> and default {}.

steps.title: Implement the override logic in mockProductBuilder
steps.instruction: Update the mockProductBuilder function to accept an optional overrides parameter and merge it with default product values using object spread syntax.
steps.hint: Add a parameter to the function with a type that allows partial Product overrides, then use spread syntax to combine defaults with overrides.
steps.expectedOutcome: The mockProductBuilder function should be updated to handle optional overrides and return a merged product object.
successCriteria: mockProductBuilder accepts an optional overrides parameter and returns a Product object with defaults merged with overrides using object spread.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the override logic in mockProductBuilder, maintaining consistency with the builder pattern.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure to add the overrides parameter and use object spread to merge defaults with overrides.
steps.feedbackWrong: The override logic isn't implemented correctly. Review how to merge objects with spread syntax in TypeScript.

steps.title: Test the typed mock data builders with sample usage
steps.instruction: Create sample usage of both builders to demonstrate type safety and override capabilities by adding a test function that calls mockUserBuilder and mockProductBuilder with different parameters.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates user and product instances using the builders, then logs or returns them to verify they work correctly.
steps.expectedOutcome: A test function is created that demonstrates using both mock data builders, showing how they generate typed objects.
successCriteria: A function named testBuilders (or similar) is defined that calls mockUserBuilder and mockProductBuilder and returns or logs the results.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a test function that demonstrates how the typed mock data builders work. This shows the type safety and functionality of your builders.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your test function actually calls both mockUserBuilder and mockProductBuilder to demonstrate their usage.
